summary: Ghost Rovers is an interactive storytelling website that introduces children aged 10–14 to 20 NASA machines left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Each machine is a character that tells its own story in a first-person diary, read aloud in its own voice. Older machines from the 1960s and 70s sound like crackly old radio broadcasts, while newer ones sound clear and modern. Kids spin 3D globes of the Moon and Mars to find machines at their real landing spots, explore a 3D solar system to find deep-space probes, take a quick quiz on every machine, follow a 57-year timeline, and play a game where they drive the Spirit rover through dust storms, a broken wheel and the sand trap that ended its mission. Every card links the engineering ("why I was sent") to the science ("what I found"). Ghost Rovers turns "space junk" into heroes, so kids learn that today's missions stand on the shoulders of these forgotten explorers.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Ghost Rovers is a free website where 20 retired NASA machines tell their own stories to kids aged 10–14. It covers 7 machines on the Moon (Apollo 11's Eagle, the Apollo 11 laser reflector, Surveyor 3, an ALSEP science station, Alan Shepard's golf balls and two Lunar Roving Vehicles), 8 on Mars (Viking 1 and 2, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight and Ingenuity) and 5 in deep space (NEAR Shoemaker, Dawn, Kepler, Pioneer 10 and Pioneer 11).

3D Moon: each picture sits at the machine's real landing spot. Grandma Moon shares extra facts.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Spin a 3D world. Kids drag to spin the Moon and Mars. The surfaces are drawn by our code using real map features (lunar maria, Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris, polar ice caps).

3D Mars with 8 machines, hosted by Uncle Mars (who sneezes dust storms).

2. Meet a machine. Clicking a machine opens its diary card. The machine tells its story in first person, read aloud in its own voice. The card links engineering to science: "Why I was sent", "What I found", "Where I am now", plus a fun fact, a quiz question and a link to its NASA page.

Surveyor 3's diary: it bounced on landing, and two years later Apollo 12 astronauts took its camera home.

3. Voices that age. Machines from the 1960s and 70s sound like crackly old radio, 2000s machines sound like light radio, and new machines sound clear.

4. Deep space in 3D. A 3D solar system shows where the deep-space probes are now: Dawn circling Ceres, NEAR Shoemaker on asteroid Eros, Kepler trailing Earth, and Pioneer 10 and 11 leaving the solar system.

5. Timeline. All 20 machines from 1967 to today, from launch or landing to last signal. The Apollo 11 laser reflector is still working!

6. Game: Spirit's Sand Trap. Kids drive Spirit across Gusev Crater, manage battery and dust, get cleaned by a dust devil, lose a wheel in 2006, discover silica soil with the dragging wheel in 2007, and get stuck at Troy in 2009, just as it really happened.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Kids usually hear only about today's missions. Ghost Rovers shows that every "abandoned" machine made a discovery that made later missions possible. Surveyor 3 proved the Moon was safe to land on, and the laser reflector still measures the Moon's distance today. It works in classrooms, at home and at outreach events, with no login or install.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

HTML, CSS and JavaScript; three.js for 3D; the Web Audio API for sound effects; Python for building the content and voices; hosted on GitHub Pages.

CREATIVITY

Machines become characters with personalities that match their real history: Ingenuity is hyper because it flew 72 times instead of 5, and Opportunity is a show-off because it drove a marathon. The voices "age" like old radio, and the game lets kids live a real mission instead of reading about it.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Accuracy: facts are based on NASA and NSSDCA pages, linked on every card.

- Age 10–14: simple words, humour, quizzes, a game and a certificate for meeting all 20 machines.

- Accessibility: every story is read aloud, machines can be opened from a list without the 3D view, and it works with keyboard, mouse and touch.

- Honest AI use: every AI image carries a visible watermark, AI voices are labelled on the page and in each audio file, and no NASA logos or flags are used in AI content.

Every AI-generated 3D image is clearly watermarked, next to real mission pictures.
